foundations.title: IPv4 Subnetting & Usable Hosts
foundations.content:
• In CIDR notation a.b.c.d / n:
  • Network bits = n.
  • Host bits = 32 - n.
  • Total IP addresses = 2^(32 - n).
  • Usable Host addresses = 2^(32 - n) - 2.
    (Subtract 2: First address is Network ID; Last address is Directed Broadcast Address).
foundations.crucial_rule: 🎯 GOLDEN RULE FOR GATE: In a /30 subnet: 2^(32-30) = 4 IPs. Minus 2 = exactly 2 usable host addresses (ideal for point-to-point router links)!

foundations.title: Fragmentation Offset Calculation Rules
foundations.content:
• Key Fragmentation Header Fields:
  • MF (More Fragments) Flag: 1 for all fragments EXCEPT the last fragment (MF = 0 for last).
  • DF (Don't Fragment) Flag: If 1 and packet exceeds MTU, packet is dropped.
  • Fragment Offset: Offset field in IPv4 header is measured in units of 8 bytes!
    Offset = (Byte offset of data) / 8.
  • Data payload in each fragment (except last) MUST be a multiple of 8 bytes!
foundations.crucial_rule: 🎯 GOLDEN RULE FOR GATE: Fragment offset is measured in units of 8 BYTES! Subtract the 20-byte IP header first: if MTU = 1500 bytes, max data payload is 1480 bytes (1480 / 8 = 185, a valid multiple of 8)!

worked_examples.title: Worked Example: IPv4 Packet Fragmentation
worked_examples.problem: An IP datagram of 4000 bytes (including 20-byte IP header) arrives at a router where MTU = 1500 bytes. Find payload size, MF flag, and offset for each fragment.
steps: Step 1: Total data = 4000 - 20 = 3980 bytes.
Step 2: Max payload per fragment = 1500 - 20 = 1480 bytes (multiple of 8).
Step 3: Frag 1: Payload = 1480 bytes, Offset = 0 / 8 = 0, MF = 1.
Step 4: Frag 2: Payload = 1480 bytes, Offset = 1480 / 8 = 185, MF = 1.
Step 5: Remaining data = 3980 - 2960 = 1020 bytes.
Step 6: Frag 3: Payload = 1020 bytes, Offset = 2960 / 8 = 370, MF = 0.
worked_examples.answer: Frag 1: 1480B, MF=1, Off=0; Frag 2: 1480B, MF=1, Off=185; Frag 3: 1020B, MF=0, Off=370.

exam_traps: Reassembly of fragments is performed ONLY at the DESTINATION host, never at intermediate routers!
Distance Vector routing suffers from Count-to-Infinity problem; solved by Split Horizon and Poison Reverse.

solved_examples.question: In TCP, slow-start threshold (ssthresh) is 32 KB. The current congestion window is 16 KB and reaches 32 KB via slow start. How many RTTs does it take to grow from 32 KB to 36 KB if MSS = 1 KB?
solved_examples.solution:
Step 1: At 32 KB, cwnd reaches ssthresh. TCP switches from Exponential Slow-Start to Linear Congestion Avoidance.
Step 2: In Congestion Avoidance, cwnd increases by 1 MSS (1 KB) per RTT.
Step 3: Growth from 32 KB to 36 KB is an increase of 4 KB.
Step 4: At 1 KB per RTT, it takes 4 RTTs.
Answer: 4 RTTs.
solved_examples.takeaway: Slow start: cwnd doubles every RTT (exponential). Congestion avoidance: cwnd increments by 1 MSS every RTT (linear additive increase).

1. CORE CONCEPTUAL FOUNDATIONS (POINT-BY-POINT STUDY GUIDE)

Crystal-clear, point-by-point explanations of core concepts with step-by-step logic, code, and key exam rules:

35.1

TCP Congestion Window Phases

• 1. Slow Start Phase:
  - Congestion Window (cwnd) starts at 1 MSS (Maximum Segment Size).
  - For every ACK received, cwnd increases by 1 MSS (effectively DOUBLES every RTT: exponential growth).
  - Continues until cwnd reaches ssthresh (slow-start threshold).

• 2. Congestion Avoidance Phase:
  - cwnd increases by 1 MSS per RTT (additive increase: linear growth).

• 3. On Loss Event:
  • Timeout (Severe Loss): ssthresh = cwnd / 2, and cwnd resets to 1 MSS (re-enters Slow Start).
  • 3 Duplicate ACKs (Mild Loss - Fast Retransmit): ssthresh = cwnd / 2, and cwnd = ssthresh (Fast Recovery).
✨
🎯 GOLDEN RULE FOR GATE: On 3 duplicate ACKs, cwnd drops to ssthresh (not 1 MSS!) and enters Congestion Avoidance. On Timeout, cwnd resets all the way down to 1 MSS!
35.2

Application Layer Protocols Summary

• DNS (Port 53): Uses UDP for standard queries (fast); uses TCP for zone transfers.
• HTTP (Port 80) / HTTPS (Port 443): Uses TCP.
  - Non-persistent HTTP/1.0: 2 RTTs per object.
  - Persistent HTTP/1.1: 1 RTT per object after initial connection handshake.
• Email Protocols:
  - SMTP (Port 25): Push protocol (client to mail server, server to server).
  - POP3 (Port 110) / IMAP (Port 143): Pull protocols (client downloading mail from server).
✨
🎯 GOLDEN RULE FOR GATE: SMTP is a PUSH protocol! POP3 and IMAP are PULL protocols! DNS uses UDP for queries but TCP for zone transfers.

2. STEP-BY-STEP EXAM WORKED EXAMPLES & PROBLEM TRACES

High-yield exam-pattern numerical and conceptual problems solved with explicit step-by-step derivations:

🔢 Step-by-Step Solved Problem

Worked Example: Tracing TCP cwnd Growth

Problem Statement: A TCP connection has ssthresh = 16 KB and MSS = 2 KB. Starting from cwnd = 2 KB, trace cwnd after 5 RTTs (no loss).
Step-by-Step Solution & Traces:
• Step 1: Round 0: cwnd = 2 KB.
• Step 2: RTT 1 (Slow Start): cwnd doubles to 4 KB.
• Step 3: RTT 2 (Slow Start): cwnd doubles to 8 KB.
• Step 4: RTT 3 (Slow Start): cwnd doubles to 16 KB (reaches ssthresh).
• Step 5: RTT 4 (Congestion Avoidance): cwnd increases linearly by 1 MSS (+2 KB) = 18 KB.
• Step 6: RTT 5 (Congestion Avoidance): cwnd increases by 1 MSS (+2 KB) = 20 KB.
✅ After 5 RTTs, cwnd = 20 KB.

3. COMMON MISCONCEPTIONS & EXAM TRAP WARNINGS

Critical negative-marking traps designed to catch unprepared candidates:

⚠️ GATE Exam Pitfall

TCP uses byte sequence numbers, NOT packet sequence numbers! If packet carries 100 bytes starting at seq 500, next packet has seq 600.

⚠️ GATE Exam Pitfall

Silently discarding packets by UDP provides zero flow or congestion control.

4. QUICK INTUITIVE MENTAL MODELS

Simple everyday analogies to connect technical concepts with natural intuition:

💡 Intuitive Mental Model

Real-Life Analogy: Highway Speed Limit & Highway Traffic Jam

• TCP Slow Start: Starting your car gently and doubling speed every block until you reach the threshold speed limit. • Congestion Avoidance: Once past the threshold, increasing speed by only 1 km/h each block to avoid crashing into traffic ahead!
callouts: On timeout, cwnd drops all the way down to 1 MSS! On 3 duplicate ACKs (Fast Retransmit/Recovery), cwnd drops only to half (ssthresh) and continues in Congestion Avoidance.
In HTTP 1.0 non-persistent connections, fetching N objects referenced in a webpage requires N + 1 separate TCP 3-way handshakes, incurring massive latency!

1. CORE CONCEPTUAL FOUNDATIONS (POINT-BY-POINT STUDY GUIDE)

Crystal-clear, point-by-point explanations of core concepts with step-by-step logic, code, and key exam rules:

36.1

Time, Speed, Distance & Relative Speed

• Fundamental Formula: Distance = Speed × Time.
• Unit Conversion: 1 km/h = 5 / 18 m/s  and  1 m/s = 18 / 5 km/h.
• Average Speed: Total Distance / Total Time.
  - If equal distances covered at speeds v1 and v2: Average Speed = 2 · v1 · v2 / (v1 + v2) (Harmonic Mean!).
• Relative Speed:
  • Moving in Opposite directions: Relative Speed = v1 + v2.
  • Moving in Same direction: Relative Speed = |v1 - v2|.
• Boats and Streams: Downstream speed = u + v; Upstream speed = u - v.
✨
🎯 GOLDEN RULE FOR GATE: Average speed is NEVER the simple arithmetic mean (v1 + v2)/2! For equal distance intervals, average speed is always 2·v1·v2 / (v1 + v2).
36.2

Time & Work (The LCM Efficiency Method)

• LCM Method: Assume Total Work = LCM of all individual completion times.
  1. Calculate 1-day efficiency = Total Work / Individual Days.
  2. Combined efficiency = Sum of individual efficiencies.
  3. Total Days = Total Work / Combined Efficiency.
• Pipes and Cisterns: Inlet pipe adds positive work (+); Outlet pipe subtracts negative work (-).
✨
🎯 GOLDEN RULE FOR GATE: Using the LCM method eliminates messy fractions completely! If A takes 12 days and B takes 18 days: Total Work = LCM(12, 18) = 36 units. Efficiency of A = 3, B = 2. Together = 36 / 5 = 7.2 days!

2. STEP-BY-STEP EXAM WORKED EXAMPLES & PROBLEM TRACES

High-yield exam-pattern numerical and conceptual problems solved with explicit step-by-step derivations:

🔢 Step-by-Step Solved Problem

Worked Example: Two Trains Crossing Each Other

Problem Statement: Two trains of lengths 120 m and 180 m travel in opposite directions at 40 km/h and 50 km/h. How many seconds do they take to pass each other?
Step-by-Step Solution & Traces:
• Step 1: Total distance = Sum of train lengths = 120 + 180 = 300 meters.
• Step 2: Relative speed in opposite directions = 40 + 50 = 90 km/h.
• Step 3: Convert speed to m/s: 90 × (5 / 18) = 25 m/s.
• Step 4: Time taken = Distance / Speed = 300 m / (25 m/s) = 12 seconds.
✅ Time taken = 12 seconds.

3. COMMON MISCONCEPTIONS & EXAM TRAP WARNINGS

Critical negative-marking traps designed to catch unprepared candidates:

⚠️ GATE Exam Pitfall

When a train crosses a pole or person, distance covered = length of train alone (pole has negligible width).

⚠️ GATE Exam Pitfall

Successive percentage discount of x% and y% is NOT (x + y)%! Equivalent discount = x + y - (xy / 100)%.

4. QUICK INTUITIVE MENTAL MODELS

Simple everyday analogies to connect technical concepts with natural intuition:

💡 Intuitive Mental Model

Real-Life Analogy: Two Taps Filling a Bathtub

• Work and Time: Tap A fills a tub in 10 minutes (rate = 1/10 per min); Tap B fills it in 15 minutes (rate = 1/15 per min). Working together, their speeds add up: 1/10 + 1/15 = 1/6, filling the tub in 6 minutes!
callouts: Example: 'Neither the teacher nor the students WERE present' (agrees with plural 'students'). 'Neither the students nor the teacher WAS present' (agrees with singular 'teacher').
In critical reasoning and comprehension questions, never import outside real-world knowledge that is not supported by the passage text!

1. CORE CONCEPTUAL FOUNDATIONS (POINT-BY-POINT STUDY GUIDE)

Crystal-clear, point-by-point explanations of core concepts with step-by-step logic, code, and key exam rules:

37.1

Clock Angle Formula

• Angle between Hour and Minute hand at H hours and M minutes:
  Angle θ = | 30 × H - (11 / 2) × M |.
• Speeds of Hands:
  • Minute hand speed: 6° per minute (360° / 60 min).
  • Hour hand speed: 0.5° per minute (30° / 60 min).
  • Relative speed: 5.5° per minute.
• Coincidence (0°): Hands coincide 22 times in 24 hours (not 24 times, due to 11-12-1 overlap).
✨
🎯 GOLDEN RULE FOR GATE: Use θ = |30H - 5.5M|! If angle is greater than 180°, reflex angle is 360° - θ.
37.2

Painted Cube Slicing Formulas

• A large cube painted on all outside faces is cut into n³ smaller equal cubes (n cuts per edge):
  1. 3 Faces Painted (Corners): ALWAYS exactly 8 cubes (for any n ≥ 2).
  2. 2 Faces Painted (Edges): 12 × (n - 2).
  3. 1 Face Painted (Face Centers): 6 × (n - 2)².
  4. 0 Faces Painted (Inner Core): (n - 2)³.
• Verification: 8 + 12(n - 2) + 6(n - 2)² + (n - 2)³ = n³.
✨
🎯 GOLDEN RULE FOR GATE: Regardless of the value of n, cubes with 3 faces painted is ALWAYS 8 (the 8 corners of the cube)!

2. STEP-BY-STEP EXAM WORKED EXAMPLES & PROBLEM TRACES

High-yield exam-pattern numerical and conceptual problems solved with explicit step-by-step derivations:

🔢 Step-by-Step Solved Problem

Worked Example: Angle between Clock Hands

Problem Statement: Find the angle between the hour hand and minute hand of a clock at 3:40.
Step-by-Step Solution & Traces:
• Step 1: Here H = 3, M = 40.
• Step 2: Formula: θ = | 30 × H - (11 / 2) × M |.
• Step 3: 30 × 3 = 90; (11 / 2) × 40 = 220.
• Step 4: θ = | 90 - 220 | = | -130 | = 130°.
✅ Angle between hands = 130°.

Critical negative-marking traps designed to catch unprepared candidates:

⚠️ GATE Exam Pitfall

In calendar problems, remember that century years like 1900 are NOT leap years unless divisible by 400 (2000 is a leap year)!

⚠️ GATE Exam Pitfall

In blood relations, never assume gender from a person's name unless explicitly stated or implied by relationship.

1. CORE CONCEPTUAL FOUNDATIONS (POINT-BY-POINT STUDY GUIDE)

Crystal-clear, point-by-point explanations of core concepts with step-by-step logic, code, and key exam rules:

38.1

Subject-Verb Agreement (Concord) Rules

• Rule 1: Either/Or & Neither/Nor: Verb agrees with the CLOSER subject.
  Example: 'Neither the manager nor the employees were present.'
• Rule 2: As well as / Together with / Along with: Verb agrees with the FIRST subject!
  Example: 'The captain, along with his crew members, was honored.'
• Rule 3: Each, Every, Everyone, Neither (alone): Strictly SINGULAR.
  Example: 'Each of the students has completed the project.'
✨
🎯 GOLDEN RULE FOR GATE: In 'A as well as B', verb follows A! In 'Either A or B', verb follows B (the nearest subject)!
38.2

Common Word Confusions in GATE

• Affect vs Effect:
  - Affect (Verb): To influence. ('The weather affected his mood').
  - Effect (Noun): The result/consequence. ('The policy had a good effect').
• Complement vs Compliment:
  - Complement: Completes or enhances something ('Bread and butter complement each other').
  - Compliment: An expression of praise ('He paid her a nice compliment').
• Principal vs Principle: Principal = head of school / main; Principle = fundamental truth / rule.
✨
🎯 GOLDEN RULE FOR GATE: Affect is almost always an Action (Verb), Effect is an End-result (Noun). Remember RAVEN: Remember Affect Verb Effect Noun!

2. STEP-BY-STEP EXAM WORKED EXAMPLES & PROBLEM TRACES

High-yield exam-pattern numerical and conceptual problems solved with explicit step-by-step derivations:

🔢 Step-by-Step Solved Problem

Worked Example: Subject-Verb Agreement Selection

Problem Statement: Choose the correct verb: 'Neither the professor nor his research students _____ (was / were) able to solve the puzzle.'
Step-by-Step Solution & Traces:
• Step 1: Identify conjunction: 'Neither ... nor ...'.
• Step 2: Rule of Proximity: The verb agrees with the subject closer to it.
• Step 3: The closer subject is 'his research students' (Plural).
• Step 4: Plural subject requires plural verb 'were'.
✅ Correct sentence: 'Neither the professor nor his research students were able to solve the puzzle.'

3. COMMON MISCONCEPTIONS & EXAM TRAP WARNINGS

Critical negative-marking traps designed to catch unprepared candidates:

⚠️ GATE Exam Pitfall

In reading comprehension, answers that use extreme words like 'always', 'never', 'only' are usually wrong unless explicitly in the text!

⚠️ GATE Exam Pitfall

An assumption is an UNSTATED premise required for the conclusion to hold true.

4. QUICK INTUITIVE MENTAL MODELS

Simple everyday analogies to connect technical concepts with natural intuition:

💡 Intuitive Mental Model

Real-Life Analogy: The Orchestra Conductor & Courtroom Evidence

• Concord: The subject and verb must play in harmony (Singular subject takes singular verb). • Critical Reasoning: Distinguishing between a confirmed fact stated in a text versus an unproven assumption made by the author.
callouts: In a cross or linear strip net of a cube, faces separated by exactly one intervening face are ALWAYS OPPOSITE to each other in 3D!
When solving paper punch problems, always reverse the punch operations in the exact reverse chronological order of folds!

foundations.title: Subject-Verb Agreement (Concord) Rules
foundations.content:
• Rule 1: Either/Or & Neither/Nor: Verb agrees with the CLOSER subject.
  Example: 'Neither the manager nor the employees were present.'
• Rule 2: As well as / Together with / Along with: Verb agrees with the FIRST subject!
  Example: 'The captain, along with his crew members, was honored.'
• Rule 3: Each, Every, Everyone, Neither (alone): Strictly SINGULAR.
  Example: 'Each of the students has completed the project.'
foundations.crucial_rule: 🎯 GOLDEN RULE FOR GATE: In 'A as well as B', verb follows A! In 'Either A or B', verb follows B (the nearest subject)!

foundations.title: Common Word Confusions in GATE
foundations.content:
• Affect vs Effect:
  - Affect (Verb): To influence. ('The weather affected his mood').
  - Effect (Noun): The result/consequence. ('The policy had a good effect').
• Complement vs Compliment:
  - Complement: Completes or enhances something ('Bread and butter complement each other').
  - Compliment: An expression of praise ('He paid her a nice compliment').
• Principal vs Principle: Principal = head of school / main; Principle = fundamental truth / rule.
foundations.crucial_rule: 🎯 GOLDEN RULE FOR GATE: Affect is almost always an Action (Verb), Effect is an End-result (Noun). Remember RAVEN: Remember Affect Verb Effect Noun!
